it's a stereotype, resting on the false idea that a vegan diet is inherently inferior; the main nutrition bodies consider well-planned vegan diets adequate. There are vegans of every kind, including elite athletes. On depression, the studies are mixed: some meta-analyses find an association between vegetarian diets and depressive symptoms, but the direction isn't clear, and there are signs that people start avoiding meat after a diagnosis, not the other way round. Part of the distress vegans report may be moral and social rather than nutritional: psychologist Clare Mann called it "vystopia", the anguish of perceiving animal suffering in a world that ignores it, a proposed concept, not a clinical diagnosis. A correlation doesn't tell us what causes what.

P1 is true: some meta-analyses find an association. So is P2. The problem lies in P3: the association doesn't show causation, and the deficiencies are preventable.
"Vegetarian diets are linked to more depression."

You can't tell what someone eats just by looking at them. There are strong vegans, athletes, doctors, artists and people of every kind. Food made only from plants, when it's varied and well thought out, gives the body what it needs. Thinking that everyone in a group is the same isn't fair, and it isn't true. And when a vegan feels sad, sometimes it's because they care a lot about animals and see that many people don't.

It's a stereotype, born of the false idea that a vegan diet is inferior: the main nutrition bodies consider well-planned vegan diets adequate, and there are vegans of every kind, including elite athletes. On depression, the results are mixed: some meta-analyses find an association, other studies don't, and the studies are mostly cross-sectional and don't show what causes what. There are signs that many people start avoiding meat after a diagnosis, not the other way round. Deficiencies in B12 or iron can affect mood, but they're preventable with planning. And part of the distress may come from elsewhere: psychologist Clare Mann calls it "vystopia", the anguish of perceiving animal suffering in a world that treats it as normal.
"If many people stop eating meat after a diagnosis, did the diet cause the depression, or the other way round?"
The argument mixes a stereotype with a statistical association:
A vegan diet is inherently inferior
False: nutrition bodies consider well-planned vegan diets adequate
Stereotype: there are vegans of every kind
There's an association between vegetarianism and depressive symptoms

Appearance doesn't reveal diet. High-level vegan athletes and vegans of all ages contradict the image (G11).

text.bold: 2. The premise that the diet is inferior is false.

paragraph.text: The stereotype assumes that without meat a diet is incomplete. The Academy of Nutrition and Dietetics, in the United States, states that well-planned vegetarian diets, including vegan ones, are healthy and nutritionally adequate at all stages of life. What matters is planning, as with any diet (G2, G3).

text.bold: 3. The results on depression are mixed, and the association doesn't show the direction.

paragraph.text: A 2022 systematic review of 23 studies found conflicting results: of the 25 outcomes analysed, 11 linked vegetarian or vegan diets to more depression, 7 to benefits and 7 to no association. Meta-analyses from 2021 found an association between vegetarian diets and depressive symptoms, but most of the studies are cross-sectional, and the authors themselves point out that it's impossible to know whether the diet leads to depression or the reverse.

text.bold: 4. There are signs of reverse causation.

paragraph.text: A longitudinal German study found that many people began avoiding meat after a diagnosis of a mental disorder. Sensitivity to others' suffering may also be linked to both factors.
A lack of B12, iron or omega-3 can affect energy and mood, but it's prevented with supplementation and planning (G4, G5, G7).

text.bold: 6. There's also a moral and social explanation: "vystopia".

paragraph.text: Clare Mann, a psychologist working in Australia, coined the term

(from "vegan" and "dystopia") to describe the anguish of becoming aware of the scale of animal suffering while living in a world that treats it as normal: isolation, anger, guilt and difficulty relating to people who don't see the same thing. She developed the idea in the book

text.italic: Vystopia: The Anguish of Being Vegan in a Non-Vegan World

paragraph.text: , published in 2018. It's a concept proposed from clinical practice, not a diagnosis recognized in psychiatric manuals. Research is still at an early stage: a 2025 study analysed more than 14,000 posts from an online forum on the subject and found accounts of strained relationships, pessimism and existential distress, linked mainly to moral concerns. If so, part of the sadness doesn't come from the plate, but from caring about those who suffer; and that isn't a sign of weakness.

Those who use the argument reject this

The association between vegetarian diets and depressive symptoms appears in some studies and deserves serious investigation. It's also true that many vegans report distress, which the idea of "vystopia" helps to name and which deserves support. Nutritional deficiencies can affect mood, and vegans should take care of them. It's also true that some vegans are in poor health, like people on any diet.
But a stereotype isn't evidence, and an association isn't a cause. With planning, a vegan diet supports healthy bodies and minds.
